title: How do you solve an operations case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete operations case guide: mapping a process, finding the bottleneck with simple maths, worked through hospital emergency waiting times.
hook: Operations cases reward a different kind of thinking: follow the work from start to finish and find the one step that holds everything up. Here is how that looks in a real-world style case, with the simple maths that proves where the bottleneck is.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet this case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example with real numbers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Phrases to use
  • Practice prompts with model answers

When you will meet this case

Operations cases: something is slow, costly or error-prone.

The structure

Which outcome matters most: cost, speed, capacity or quality?
  • Map it
    • Steps and hand-offs
    • Time, cost and errors at each step
    • The bottleneck
  • Fix the steps (known as ECRS; technology often does the simplifying)
    • Eliminate
    • Combine
    • Re-order
    • Simplify
  • Fix what supports them
    • People (skills · incentives · staffing)
    • Technology and systems

The slowest step (the bottleneck) sets the output of the whole process. Speeding up any other step adds nothing, so fix the bottleneck first, then check which step becomes the new one.

A fully worked example

The prompt: a hospital's emergency department waiting times have doubled in a year. Why?

Step 1: map the flow. Arrive, triage, see a doctor, tests, decision, then either go home or be admitted to a ward bed.

Step 2: check each stage. Arrivals are up only 5%, and staffing is unchanged, so demand alone does not explain doubling waits.

Step 3: look at the exit. About 300 patients arrive a day, and a quarter, 75, need a ward bed. Ward discharges mostly happen late in the afternoon, so admitted patients now wait about 6 extra hours in the emergency department for a bed.

Step 4: put a number on it. 75 patients × 6 hours = 450 bed-hours a day. Divided by 24 hours, that is like having about 19 cubicles permanently blocked. New arrivals have nowhere to be seen, so everyone waits.

Recommendation: "The bottleneck is not the emergency department itself but beds upstairs: admitted patients occupy the equivalent of 19 cubicles while waiting. I'd move ward discharges earlier in the day, add a discharge lounge, and work with social care to speed up patients waiting to go home. Adding emergency staff alone would not fix it."

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Asking for more staff without checking where the delay actually happens.
  2. Analysing every step equally instead of finding the bottleneck.
  3. Not putting a number on the bottleneck to prove it matters.
  4. Fixing a step that is not the constraint, which changes nothing overall.

Phrases to use

Let me follow a patient from arrival to leaving and see where the time goes.
Speeding up any other step adds nothing until we fix the bottleneck.

Practise with these prompts

A hospital's emergency waiting times have doubled in a year.

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Number of arrivals, by hour and day; Case mix: older, sicker patients take longer
  • Capacity: Doctors and nurses on shift vs arrivals; Cubicles and beds in the department
  • Process inside the department: Triage, tests, waiting for a specialist; Handovers between shifts
  • Flow out: Waiting for a ward bed upstairs; Discharges and social care delays

Where to start: Flow out: in most hospitals, patients waiting for a ward bed block the emergency department.

The trap: Only asking for more staff without checking whether patients are stuck waiting for beds.

A parcel company's on-time delivery fell from 95% to 85%.

Show a model structure
  • Where in the chain: Collection, sorting hub, linehaul, last mile; Which step has the delays?
  • Volume vs capacity: Parcel volume growth vs vans, drivers, sorting hours; Peaks by day and season
  • Process and systems: Route planning, scanning, missed handovers; New system or new hub recently?
  • External: Weather, traffic, partner carriers; Customer address and access problems

Where to start: Where in the chain: find the step where parcels start running late.

The trap: Listing causes without locating where in the chain delays start.

An airline's aircraft spend 20% longer on the ground between flights than rivals'.

Show a model structure
  • Arrival: Waiting for a gate, stand or tug; Taxi times
  • Aircraft servicing: Cleaning, catering, fuel, bags; Which task is on the critical path?
  • Boarding: Boarding process, cabin bags; Late passengers
  • Planning: Schedule buffers, crew connections; Staff numbers at peak

Where to start: The critical path: the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another sets the turnaround, so speeding up steps off that chain does nothing.

The trap: Trying to speed up every task when only the ones on the critical path matter.

A bottleneck calculation that changes the answer

A hospital's outpatient clinic has two stages. Three nurses each complete a 15-minute intake, giving combined capacity of 12 patients per hour. Two doctors each complete a 20-minute consultation, giving combined capacity of 6 patients per hour. If eight patients arrive each hour for several hours, the waiting line grows at approximately two patients per hour once the doctor's queue is saturated.

Hiring another intake nurse will not solve the long wait, because intake is not the constraint. Adding one doctor increases consultation capacity from six to nine patients per hour, potentially eliminating the accumulating queue during those hours. But this simplified result assumes constant service times, sufficient rooms and support staff, and no downstream discharge constraint.

If the clinic instead reduces unnecessary doctor appointments by safely routing 25% of visits to an appropriate nurse-led pathway, demand on doctors falls from eight to six an hour. That could also remove the average capacity deficit, but patient suitability and clinical quality must be tested. In a case interview, lay out both the arithmetic and the operational conditions before declaring the problem solved.

A strong operational recommendation names the bottleneck, quantifies the expected effect, identifies implementation constraints and proposes a pilot with throughput, wait-time and quality measures. Optimising a non-bottleneck step may make that team look more productive while leaving the customer experience unchanged.
